# Hedge growing into the sightline at AWS-04

Noticed on this weekend's round that the hedge along the eastern boundary
at AWS-04 has grown enough over the last year that it's now clipping the
bottom of the radio path toward the AWS-05 repeater hop. Nothing has
dropped out yet as far as I can tell from the logs, but the margin that
used to be there when the mast was first put up has visibly closed, and
hedges don't stop growing on their own.

## What it looked like on site

Standing at the base of the AWS-04 mast and sighting up toward where the
antenna points, the hedge line now sits noticeably higher than it did in
the photos from the original install, close enough that the top few inches
of new growth were swaying into the line of sight in the wind while I stood
there. It isn't blocking the path outright, but it's close enough that
another season's growth would.

## Why this matters for the mast, not just the radio

The mast at AWS-04 was originally sited partly because of that same
sightline — enough height was chosen to clear the hedge as it stood at
install, without going taller than it needed to be for a farm boundary
that's supposed to stay low. If the hedge keeps closing the gap, the choice
becomes trimming the hedge, which isn't ours to do without asking the
landowner, or raising the mast, which is a bigger job than a fence-line trim
and changes the guying calculations done for the original height.

## What I'm proposing

Raise it with the landowner at AWS-04 before the next trim is due anyway,
since a friendly ask about keeping that section a bit lower costs nothing
and avoids either side being surprised later. In parallel, worth checking
the AWS-05 hop's frame-loss figures over the last few months to see whether
there's already a measurable trend, rather than waiting until the sightline
is fully blocked to find out the hard way.

## Loose end

Haven't measured the actual clearance in any rigorous way, just eyeballed
it against old photos, so this is a heads-up rather than a finished
assessment. Someone with a tape measure and a ladder would get a much
better number than I did standing at the base looking up.
